title: 四级试卷 01 · 技术与合作
description: 原创模拟试卷，包含完整非听力题量：写作、选词填空、长篇阅读、仔细阅读和翻译。

sections.title: 写作
sections.instructions: 建议用时 30 分钟。按题目要求写一篇 120–180 词的短文。
study_paragraphs: A useful campus library should make routine tasks easy without making students feel that they are speaking only to machines. I propose a simple online reservation system for group study rooms. Students could see available times and receive a reminder before their booking. This would reduce queues and help them plan meetings. However, the library should also keep a desk where students can ask a person for help. New users may not understand the system, and some students may need special arrangements. Staff could collect common questions and use them to improve the website. The university should test the service in one building first and invite feedback after a month. Technology would then support a better service rather than become the only way to receive it.

questions.prompt: Write 120–180 words proposing one way for a campus library to use technology while keeping personal help available.

questions.explanation: 核对是否提出具体措施、解释用途并讨论人工支持；范文采用“建议—好处—边界—试点”的结构。

sections.title: 选词填空（26–35）
sections.instructions: 从 A–O 的 15 个词中选择 10 个填入空白处，每词最多使用一次。

A worker still checked each delivery, because a machine could not judge whether a damaged book needed [3] ______ handling. After two weeks, the service became more [4] ______. The lesson was simple: a new device creates value only when people can [5] ______ how to use it.

To learn what students really needed, the library compared delivery [6] ______ with comments collected at the help desk. Some students wanted to [7] ______ books late in the evening, while others simply needed clearer directions during the day. Instead of buying more machines immediately, staff introduced [8] ______ checks of the signs and messages. They also invited students who had not used the service before to try it without instructions from a librarian. An [9] ______ user could often discover a confusing step that an experienced worker no longer noticed.

study_paragraphs: When a college bought a machine to carry books, staff expected an immediate improvement. Instead, students were confused by the pickup messages. The library invited them to describe the problem and then changed the signs. A worker still checked each delivery, because a machine could not judge whether a damaged book needed careful handling. After two weeks, the service became more reliable. The lesson was simple: a new device creates value only when people can understand how to use it.

To learn what students really needed, the library compared delivery records with comments collected at the help desk. Some students wanted to borrow books late in the evening, while others simply needed clearer directions during the day. Instead of buying more machines immediately, staff introduced regular checks of the signs and messages. They also invited students who had not used the service before to try it without instructions from a librarian. An independent user could often discover a confusing step that an experienced worker no longer noticed.

At the first meeting, several shy students remained silent until a volunteer asked them to write their suggestions on cards. Their comments showed that a convenient service needed more than fast equipment. It needed patient communication, opportunities to report problems and a clear way to get help when something went wrong. The final design combined automated delivery with a small team of people who could explain unfamiliar steps.

questions.explanation: be confused by 表示“对……感到困惑”，与随后修改标识的情境对应。
invite somebody to 后接动词原形；describe the problem 表示描述问题。
handling 为名词，前面需要形容词；破损书籍需要 careful handling。
become 后用形容词作表语；改进后的服务更加 reliable。
can 后接动词原形；understand how to use it 表示理解使用方法。
delivery records 是“配送记录”；compare A with B 表示比较两类信息。
want to 后接动词原形；borrow books 表示借书。
checks 为名词，regular checks 表示定期检查。
an 后面需要以元音音素开头的修饰语；独立尝试的新用户能发现工作人员忽略的问题。
remained 后接形容词作表语；直到被邀请写卡片前，害羞的学生保持 silent。

sections.title: 长篇阅读（36–45）· 校园共享
sections.instructions: 阅读 A–L 段，将每条陈述与对应段落匹配。段落可以重复使用。
paragraphs: [A] The repair club meets on Friday afternoons. Students bring broken lamps or bags instead of throwing them away. Before anyone touches a tool, a volunteer explains the basic safety rules. Some items cannot be repaired, but visitors still learn why they failed. The club keeps a notebook describing each repair, including those that do not succeed. Its purpose is not to promise that every object will work again. Instead, organisers want students to recognise when an item can be repaired safely and when professional help is necessary. Visitors may watch before deciding whether to join.

[B] The food-sharing team posts an ingredient list beside every donated meal. People can choose what suits them and leave unsuitable food for someone else. The team asks donors to label the time of preparation as well. Clear information matters more than a large number of donations. Donations are accepted only during a short period before the evening meal, and volunteers check the storage temperature. A notice explains that anyone may collect a portion without giving a reason. This prevents the service from turning a useful exchange into an uncomfortable test of personal need.

[C] The evening walking group welcomes students who dislike competitive sports. Nobody records a finishing time, and the route has several places to rest. Members usually talk about classes while walking. The organiser believes that a comfortable first experience makes returning easier. The leader changes the meeting point occasionally so that students from different buildings can join easily. After each walk, members may suggest a shorter or quieter route. Their feedback has shaped the activity more than the original plan. Returning participants are encouraged to welcome newcomers rather than set the pace.

[D] A small lending shelf holds umbrellas and chargers. Borrowers write down what they take and return it when finished. At the end of each week, volunteers check which items are missing or broken. The records help them decide what to buy next. One month, the shelf contained many umbrellas but only two working chargers. The lending records showed that chargers were borrowed far more often. Volunteers therefore spent the next small donation on chargers instead of adding more umbrellas. They also attached clear return instructions so that new borrowers did not need to find an organiser.

[E] At the start of term, two students proposed a website listing every sharing activity on campus. A trial version offered only opening times, locations and contact details. Students liked being able to check whether a service was available before crossing the campus. The designers decided to keep those basic details easy to find rather than add a complicated reward system. A volunteer now contacts organisers each week to update information. The site is useful because its small amount of information is dependable.

[F] A language exchange began with public presentations, but several beginners stopped attending. Organisers then divided participants into pairs and offered a few everyday topics to discuss. Students could practise a conversation once before speaking to a new partner. Mistakes were treated as part of learning, and nobody was required to perform in front of the whole group. Attendance improved after this change. The organisers concluded that an activity can be open to everyone on paper while still making some people feel unable to take part.

[G] The gardening team originally asked each member to water the vegetables whenever they had time. Some plants received water twice a day while others received none. A simple weekly timetable solved much of the problem. Each task had one named volunteer and a person who could take over if necessary. Members could exchange days by updating the timetable. The garden did not need more enthusiastic promises; it needed a shared picture of work that was easy for everyone to check.

[H] During the first month of a clothing exchange, posters celebrated the number of donated items. Volunteers later realised that this number said little about how useful the service was. They began recording how many items actually found new owners and asking whether sizes were missing. An impressive pile of unsuitable clothes could hide a poor result. By measuring successful exchanges, the team could plan collection days around what students needed instead of collecting as much as possible.

[I] A bicycle workshop offered evening appointments through an online form. When the website briefly stopped working, students assumed that the workshop had closed. Organisers added a telephone number and a noticeboard beside the entrance. Online booking remained convenient, but students now had another route to help. The workshop also reserved a few appointments for people who arrived without booking. Its volunteers learned that introducing technology creates a responsibility to consider what happens when that technology is unavailable.

[J] A student survey asked which campus services were most popular. Almost all replies came from people who already used the main library, because the survey link was displayed there. A volunteer pointed out that the result could not reveal why other students stayed away. The team then collected responses in different buildings and at different times. The additional answers did not simply make the survey larger. They brought in experiences that the original method had left out.

[K] Volunteers who ran the lending shelf sometimes received requests for services they had never promised to provide. A short guide now explains which items can be borrowed, how long a loan lasts and who handles damaged equipment. The guide also describes how a borrower can suggest a new item. These boundaries have reduced disagreement without stopping useful ideas. Organisers believe that sharing works best when participants understand both what they may expect and what responsibilities they accept.

[L] A campus sharing fair brought the different groups together at the end of term. Visitors could try a short activity before signing up, and organisers displayed both achievements and problems. The most valuable discussions often concerned a change that had failed. Groups discovered that a method useful for one service might not suit another. They agreed to exchange notes next term, but each group would test proposed improvements with its own participants rather than copy another activity without examining its needs.

questions.prompt: 36. The group reduces pressure on beginners by avoiding competition.
questions.explanation: C 段明确没有计时和竞争，允许休息，并让回访成员照顾新参与者。

questions.prompt: 37. Participants receive safety instructions before using equipment.
questions.explanation: A 段说明碰工具之前由志愿者讲解基本安全规则。

questions.prompt: 38. Borrowing records help volunteers decide which equipment to purchase.
questions.explanation: D 段用借用记录比较充电器与雨伞需求，并据此购买充电器。

questions.prompt: 39. People can collect food without explaining why they need it.
questions.explanation: B 段强调领取者不必说明理由，避免让分享服务成为对个人需要的审查。

questions.prompt: 40. The designers favour reliable basic information over additional features.
questions.explanation: E 段保留易查的时间、地点和联系方式，没有增加复杂奖励系统。

questions.prompt: 41. Replacing public performances with pair work helped people return.
questions.explanation: F 段从公开展示改为两人练习，随后出勤改善。

questions.prompt: 42. A schedule identifies both the person responsible and a possible replacement.
questions.explanation: G 段为每项工作安排一名负责者和必要时的替补。

questions.prompt: 43. The team changed its measure of success from donations to completed exchanges.
questions.explanation: H 段不再只统计捐赠量，改为记录实际找到新主人的物品。

questions.prompt: 44. The service provides another way to obtain help when online booking fails.
questions.explanation: I 段在网站故障后增加电话、公告栏以及现场预约名额。

questions.prompt: 45. The original survey missed people whose experiences differed from regular users.
questions.explanation: J 段最初只在图书馆征集答复，后来到不同建筑和时段补充调查。

sections.title: 仔细阅读 · Passage One（46–50）
sections.instructions: 阅读文章，为每题选择一个最佳答案。
paragraphs: Nora wanted to buy vegetables for a student cooking class. One shop displayed attractive green labels on every packet. Another provided a plain list showing where each vegetable came from and when it had arrived. The green labels looked impressive, but they did not answer Nora's questions about freshness or price.

She compared the vegetables themselves, asked about delivery times and chose a mixture from both shops. Later, she showed the class her receipts. Some students were surprised that there was no single label they could follow. Nora explained that useful information had to match the decision being made. A label might tell buyers something important, but it could not replace every other question.

During the discussion, one student argued that a trusted label saved time. Nora agreed. Buyers could not investigate every detail of every product, and reliable standards could make some choices easier. However, the class was planning a meal for the following day, so delivery time mattered alongside the method of production. A label that answered one question did not necessarily answer the question that was most urgent for this meal. The students began to distinguish between information that was useful in general and information that directly served a particular purpose.

For the next class, they made a short checklist before visiting the shops. It included price, quantity, arrival date and whether the vegetables would keep well overnight. They also agreed that they could revise the checklist if a new need appeared. The exercise did not lead them to reject labels or favour one seller permanently. It taught them to decide what they needed to know before allowing the most attractive message in the shop to guide their attention. They found that the checklist also helped them explain their choices to one another. Discussion became more specific because students could compare the same features instead of arguing about which label looked more convincing.

questions.prompt: 46. Why did the green labels fail to satisfy Nora?

options.text: They offered no explanation of the production method.
They left her questions about freshness and price unanswered.
They showed that all the vegetables had arrived too late.
They required her to purchase only one type of vegetable.

questions.explanation: 首段说明标签没有回答她关于新鲜程度和价格的问题。

questions.prompt: 47. What did Nora do before making her purchase?

options.text: She chose the shop with the widest range of labels.
She followed the recommendation of the other students.
She removed products that came from unfamiliar farms.
She compared the vegetables and asked about delivery times.

questions.explanation: 第二段直接描述比较蔬菜并询问配送时间，最后从两家店选购。

questions.prompt: 48. How does Nora respond to the claim that trusted labels save time?

options.text: She accepts their value while pointing out their limits.
She says they should replace all direct questions to sellers.
She believes they matter only when shoppers have enough time.
She argues that every label requires a full investigation.

questions.explanation: 第三段先认可可靠标准能帮助选择，再指出标签无法回答所有与当前用餐相关的问题。

questions.prompt: 49. Why was the arrival date important to the cooking class?

options.text: The class intended to compare farms over several months.
The vegetables would be displayed rather than cooked.
The students needed food suitable for a meal the next day.
The shop offered a lower price for the newest deliveries.

questions.explanation: 第三段交代翌日用餐这一具体目的，末段还要求蔬菜能保存过夜。

questions.prompt: 50. What is the main lesson of the shopping exercise?

options.text: Choosing one trusted seller removes the need for planning.
The largest amount of information always leads to the best choice.
Attractive product messages usually contain false information.
Relevant information should be judged against the purpose of a decision.

questions.explanation: 全文强调先明确当前决策所需的信息，再评价标签及其他信息，而非一概拒绝标签。

sections.title: 仔细阅读 · Passage Two（51–55）
sections.instructions: 阅读文章，为每题选择一个最佳答案。
paragraphs: Four students organised a weekend book sale. Each selected an enjoyable task, such as designing posters or arranging books. Nobody volunteered to carry the boxes home afterwards. When the sale ended, the boxes remained beside the entrance, and everyone thought someone else would remove them.

For the next event, the group listed every job before dividing the work. They paired popular tasks with less popular ones and allowed members to exchange assignments. They also agreed on a final check before leaving. The change did not require anyone to become more generous overnight. It made the responsibilities visible, so a willing team could turn good intentions into finished work.

Before the second sale, the students asked the building manager which rules they had overlooked. They learned that the entrance had to be cleared by a fixed time and that leftover books needed a temporary storage place. These details were added to the list. The group also estimated how long each job would take. Carrying boxes was less appealing than making posters, but it was not necessarily more time-consuming. Sharing information about the work made it easier to divide tasks in a way that members considered fair.

On the day of the event, one student had to leave early for a family appointment. Because everyone could see the plan, another member took over the final delivery and the list was updated immediately. The event ended with all the books stored and the entrance clear. Afterwards, the team kept the checklist for future volunteers, adding a note about what had changed. They concluded that a plan should make adjustments easier rather than force people to follow arrangements that no longer fit the situation. New members later used the notes to prepare another sale. They still discussed their own availability, but they could begin with a complete picture of the work instead of discovering missing responsibilities after the event.

questions.prompt: 51. Why were the boxes left at the entrance after the first sale?

options.text: The library had asked the students to display them there.
The group was waiting for buyers who arrived later.
Nobody had been given responsibility for removing them.
The students had decided to postpone every cleaning task.

questions.explanation: 首段说明没有人认领搬走箱子的工作，大家以为别人会完成。

questions.prompt: 52. What was the main change made for the next event?

options.text: The group listed all jobs and assigned responsibility for them.
Members could choose only tasks they already enjoyed.
One student was required to perform every remaining task.
The team avoided tasks that required contact with the manager.

questions.explanation: 第二段先列出全部工作，再分配并允许交换，结束前进行检查。

questions.prompt: 53. What additional information did the building manager provide?

options.text: Which poster designs had attracted the most customers.
The deadline for clearing the entrance and the need for storage.
How many books each student was expected to sell.
Why the sale should be moved to a different weekend.

questions.explanation: 第三段新增两项限制：入口须按时清空，剩余书籍需有临时存放地点。

questions.prompt: 54. What does the early departure of one student demonstrate?

options.text: A shared plan can help members adjust responsibilities.
Family appointments should always take priority over teamwork.
Replacing a member usually requires cancelling the event.
A detailed checklist prevents people from changing their plans.

questions.explanation: 末段展示其他成员能够看到计划并及时接替工作，说明计划支持调整。

questions.prompt: 55. Which statement best describes the author's view of a useful plan?

options.text: It should ensure that all tasks are equally enjoyable.
It should remain unchanged once everyone has agreed to it.
It should replace discussion between the people involved.
It should clarify duties while allowing necessary changes.

questions.explanation: 全文强调明确责任；末句又强调计划应方便调整，而非强迫遵守不再合适的安排。

sections.title: 翻译 · 中译英
sections.instructions: 建议用时 30 分钟。将下面的中文段落译成英文，注意信息完整和表达连贯。
paragraphs: 校园里的一间旧教室被改造成了共享修理室。学生可以在志愿者的帮助下修理日常用品，也可以把不再使用的工具捐给其他人。这个小空间不仅减少了浪费，还让不同专业的学生有机会一起解决实际问题。修理室每周开放两次，并提供简单的预约服务。遇到无法解决的问题时，志愿者会记录情况，再向有经验的老师请教。学校计划根据学生的建议逐步完善这里的设施，使更多人愿意参与资源共享。
study_paragraphs: An old classroom on campus has been turned into a shared repair room. Students can repair everyday items with help from volunteers, or donate tools they no longer use. This small space reduces waste and gives students from different majors a chance to solve practical problems together. The repair room opens twice a week and offers a simple booking service. When volunteers cannot solve a problem, they record the details and ask experienced teachers for advice. questions.answer: An old classroom on campus has been turned into a shared repair room. Students can repair everyday items with help from volunteers, or donate tools they no longer use. This small space reduces waste and gives students from different majors a chance to solve practical problems together. The repair room opens twice a week and offers a simple booking service. When volunteers cannot solve a problem, they record the details and ask experienced teachers for advice. The university plans to improve the facilities gradually in response to students' suggestions, encouraging more people to take part in sharing resources.
